rows.description: One toddler cries in a nursery and others begin to cry or look worried without knowing why. Emotions pass quickly between very young children.

rows.subtype: Laughter and panic in a class [Actor]
rows.description: A giggle spreads through a classroom until nobody can stop, or a rumour of an exam change spreads worry through everyone. Feelings move through groups faster than facts.

rows.subtype: Absorbing the crowd's excitement or fear [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager at a match, concert or rally is swept up in the crowd's energy, feeling joy or anger that is not entirely their own. Shared feeling can be warm and can make them act unusually.

A toddler climbs into a lap, cuddles or holds a hand to seek comfort and closeness. This is a core way of feeling safe; warm, responsive touch supports secure attachment, and a child who pulls away should be respected.

A gentle stroke of the hand or hair between partners or close family conveys tenderness. It is welcome only with clear consent and context; if the other person stiffens or pulls away, stop and check in.

rows.subtype: Handshake and greeting in work life [Expressing]
rows.description: A young professional shakes hands, offers a namaste or a nod according to setting, gender norms and health needs. A firm, brief handshake conveys respect, but preferences differ, so following the other person's lead is wise.
A parent says telling the truth matters more than the mistake, and responds to a confession with calm repair and thanks. Asking traps such as who did this is avoided, since they invite lying.
Children watch adults tell white lies on the phone, or brag, or cheat on small rules. Adults who own their own errors openly teach more about honesty than any lecture does.

A child sees police as scary figures, told by adults that they will take you away if you misbehave. Fear teaches little; explaining that police are there to help, and to be cautious yet respectful, is healthier.
A driver at a checkpoint faces a fine and a hint of settling on the spot. Paying the official fine with a receipt is lawful; offering money privately is a bribe and risks more trouble.
A toddler rubs eyes, whines, clings or melts down when overtired. Tiredness is often mistaken for naughtiness, and sleep or rest fixes many tantrums.
A child with a calm resting face is neither happy nor sad. A neutral face is not a sign of anger or disinterest, and adults avoid over-reading it.

rows.subtype: Bored and tired in study life [Expressing]
rows.description: A young adult in a dull lecture or overloaded semester shows yawns, doodling and phone use. Boredom, tiredness and poor sleep overlap, and structure, breaks and rest help.
A toddler with dropped, loose shoulders in a caregiver's arms shows safety and relaxation, and tense shoulders may show distress or pain.
A child drops the shoulders after a loss or disappointing marks, showing sadness or defeat. A warm word helps more than telling the child to cheer up.
An adult shrugs with palms up to show helplessness or an apology, but if used to dodge responsibility it can feel dismissive. Adding words shows ownership.
